A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Card, wording: The last line says the methods 'count the same ballots in different ways', but the card itself says first-past-the-post voters mark one candidate while preferential voters rank all of them, so the ballots are not the same. Something like 'the same voters' choices can lead to different results' would avoid this.

rejected.title: Voting methods
card: First-past-the-post
Voters mark one candidate, and the candidate with the most votes wins, even without more than half of all votes.
Preferential

Voters rank candidates in order, 1, 2, 3 and so on. If no one has more than half the votes, the last-placed candidate is dropped and their votes go to the voters' next choice. This repeats until one candidate has a majority.
Proportional
Seats are shared out according to each party's share of the votes. A party with about a third of the votes wins about a third of the seats. The Australian Senate uses this approach.
The methods count the same ballots in different ways, so the same votes can lead to different results.
rejected.remember: First-past-the-post: most votes wins. Preferential: rank and pass on votes. Proportional: seats match vote share.

a.q: Which method has voters rank the candidates in order of choice?
opts: Preferential voting
First-past-the-post voting
Proportional voting
Compulsory voting
a.why: Preferential voting asks voters to number candidates, so a vote can pass to the next choice. First-past-the-post is the tempting wrong answer, but voters mark only one candidate and no ranking is used.
a.clue: Think about which method uses numbers 1, 2, 3 on the ballot.

b.q: In a town election, Priya gets 40 votes, Sam gets 35 and Lee gets 25. Under first-past-the-post, who wins, and why?
opts: Priya, because she has the most votes
Priya, because she has over half the votes
Sam, because Lee's votes pass to him
No one, because no one has over half the votes
b.why: First-past-the-post gives the win to the candidate with the most votes, and Priya has 40. Saying no one wins yet, or that Lee's votes pass to Sam, applies preferential counting, where a majority is needed. First-past-the-post needs no majority, and 40 of 100 votes is not over half anyway.
b.clue: Does this method need more than half the votes?

card: First-past-the-post
Voters mark one candidate, and the candidate with the most votes wins, even without more than half of all votes.
Preferential

Voters rank candidates in order, 1, 2, 3 and so on, to elect one winner. If no one has more than half the votes, the last-placed candidate is dropped and their votes go to each voter's next choice. This repeats until one candidate has a majority.
Proportional

Several members are elected at once, and seats are shared out by each party's share of the votes. A party with about a third of the votes wins about a third of the seats. The Australian Senate uses this approach.
The same voters' choices can lead to different results, depending on which method is used.
